prompt: In the OSV entry for GO-2022-1059, which field narrows the problem in `golang.org/x/text` down to `MatchStrings` and `ParseAcceptLanguage`?
hint: There are three levels in an entry, and this is the innermost.

choices.text: `aliases`
choices.why: `aliases` lists the other names of the same problem, a CVE number and a GitHub advisory. It says nothing about code.

choices.text: `ranges`, with its `introduced` and `fixed` events
choices.why: The range is the module level: which versions, from `0` up to but not including `0.3.8`. Every function of every package is inside it.

choices.text: `ecosystem_specific.imports[].symbols`
choices.why: Right. Under the package path `golang.org/x/text/language`, `symbols` names the two functions the fix changed, and that list is what reachability is checked against.

choices.text: `package.name`
choices.why: That is the module, `golang.org/x/text`: the coarsest of the three levels.

prompt: `govulncheck -version` prints `Go: go1.27.1` on its first line. Which Go is that?
hint: Think about which standard library a source scan judges.

choices.text: The Go that compiled the `govulncheck` binary in `~/go/bin`
choices.why: A plausible reading, and not what the line reports. A source scan judges the standard library you build with, so it asks the go command on your `PATH`.

choices.text: The go command found on `PATH`
choices.why: Right. It runs `go env GOVERSION`, and that release's standard library is what the scan checks; with `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.2` the same scan found nothing.

choices.text: The version in the `go` line of the current `go.mod`
choices.why: `go.mod` says the oldest Go the module accepts. The scan uses the toolchain that will actually build it.

choices.text: The newest Go release the database has entries for
choices.why: The database is not a Go release. Its address is the third line, `DB: https://vuln.go.dev`.

prompt: Put what `govulncheck` checks for GO-2022-1059 in order, from the broadest statement to the most precise one.
hint: The OSV entry is read from the outside in, and reachability comes last.
items: the module `golang.org/x/text` is required at a version below `0.3.8`
a function the entry names, such as `ParseAcceptLanguage`, is in the call graph
a path of calls from `main` reaches that function

prompt: You run `govulncheck ./...` on a library module: no `main` package, only exported functions other people call. Where does the call graph start?
hint: The lesson named the entry points for both kinds of package.

choices.text: Nowhere, so a library can only ever have package-level findings
choices.why: A library would then be clean by construction. `govulncheck` treats its public surface as the place calls come from.

choices.text: At its tests, which play the part of `main`
choices.why: Test files are left out unless you pass `-test`, and even then they add entry points; they do not replace the exported API.

choices.text: At every exported function and method, and the `init` functions
choices.why: Right. Any of them may be called by a program you never see, so each counts as an entry point, and a path from one to a named function is a symbol-level finding.

choices.text: At the `main` of whichever program imported it most recently
choices.why: `govulncheck` sees only the code in front of it. It knows nothing about the programs that will import the library.

prompt: `accept` and `tag` both import `golang.org/x/text/language` at v0.3.7. `govulncheck ./accept` exits 3 and `govulncheck ./tag` exits 0. What separates them?
hint: Look at which function of the package each one calls.

choices.text: `accept` imports the package directly and `tag` gets it indirectly
choices.why: Both import `golang.org/x/text/language` in their own source; the import lines are identical.

choices.text: Only `accept` reaches `ParseAcceptLanguage`
choices.why: Right. `main` calls `preferred`, which calls a function GO-2022-1059 names. `tag` calls `language.Parse`, which the entry does not name, so its finding stays at the package level.

choices.text: `tag` was scanned with an older copy of the database
choices.why: Both scans used the same `-db file:///home/ana/vulndb`, a minute apart.

choices.text: `tag` handles its error from `language.Parse`, and a handled error makes the call safe
choices.why: `accept` checks its error too. `govulncheck` asks whether the function is reached, not what happens to its result.

prompt: `govulncheck -show verbose ./tag` listed 14 entries under Module Results. Two were in other packages of `golang.org/x/text`. How many of the 14 were in the standard library of Go 1.27.1?
hint: The two `golang.org/x/text` entries were GO-2026-6629 and GO-2026-5970.

prompt: On Linux, a source scan of `tag` lists GO-2026-6604, marked `Platforms: windows`, under Package Results. Why does a Windows bug appear at all?
hint: Compare with what the scan of the built binary did with the same entry.

choices.text: With no target system, nothing is filtered by platform
choices.why: Right. Source is not tied to one system, so the scan lists the entry and marks the platform. The binary, which records `GOOS=linux`, dropped it from its count.

choices.text: Every program imports `os`, so it is always counted
choices.why: Importing `os` puts it at the package level; the platform line is about which systems the bug exists on, and the binary scan left it out.

choices.text: `govulncheck` guessed that `tag` will be cross-compiled
choices.why: Nothing in the module says so, and `govulncheck` does not guess intentions; it simply does not filter source by platform.

choices.text: The local copy of the database lost its platform field
choices.why: The field is there: the output prints `Platforms: windows` from it.

prompt: The default report shows one step of the call path. `govulncheck -show ___ ./accept` prints all of it: `main`, then `preferred`, then `ParseAcceptLanguage` in `parse.go`.
hint: The plural of the word the report uses for a call path.

prompt: `accept-bin` scanned with `-mode binary` reported 1 vulnerability. The same program built with `-ldflags="-s -w"` reported 15. What happened?
hint: Ask what the binary scan reads, and what `-s -w` removes.

choices.text: No symbol table, so every vulnerable symbol of every module
choices.why: Right. Stripping removed every function name, so with nothing to look names up in, it falls back to module-level precision, and twelve standard-library entries `accept` never imports joined the list.

choices.text: The smaller binary uses different code that really is vulnerable
choices.why: `-s -w` removes debugging and symbol information; the machine code that runs is the same.

choices.text: The linker kept more functions
choices.why: The stripped file is smaller, 1,740,960 bytes against 2,683,796. Nothing was added.

choices.text: The build record was removed, so the versions were guessed
choices.why: The versions in the output are the real ones, `v0.3.7` and `go1.27.1`; the build record survives `-s -w`.

prompt: A CI step runs `govulncheck -format json ./... > vulns.json` and uploads the file. Months later somebody notices a symbol-level finding in it that the job never flagged. Why did the step stay green?

choices.text: Symbol-level findings only appear in the text output
choices.why: The JSON had it: a finding whose first frame names a function, exactly as the `jq` filter picked out.

choices.text: Redirecting the output with `>` hides the exit status
choices.why: A redirection sends standard output to a file; the exit status still reaches the shell, as `echo $?` showed.

choices.text: JSON output always exits 0, findings or not
choices.why: Right. The same holds for `sarif` and `openvex`. A job that writes JSON has to read the findings itself, or run a second, text scan for the exit status.

choices.text: CI runners cannot reach vuln.go.dev
choices.why: Then the scan would have failed with an error, and there would have been no findings in the file at all.

prompt: Match each SARIF `level` that `govulncheck -format sarif` wrote with the finding it stands for.
hint: The scan of `accept` gave 1 error, 1 warning and 14 notes.

pairs.right: a vulnerable function is reached from your code
a vulnerable package is imported, none of its named functions called
a vulnerable module is required, its package never imported

right_distractors: the scan could not load the packages

prompt: `govulncheck ./...` on lesson 1's `hits` exits 0 with "affected by 0 vulnerabilities". `govulncheck -scan module` on the same code exits 3 with "may be affected by 13". Which reading is right?
hint: What does each level look at?

choices.text: The module scan is right, and the symbol scan missed 13 calls
choices.why: Nothing was traced at the module level, which is why it says "may". The symbol scan looked for paths of calls and found none.

choices.text: Both are right: no call reaches a named function, and Go 1.27.1 has 13 entries
choices.why: Right. The module level counts every entry for the modules and the Go release in use; `hits` calls none of them. The exit status follows the level asked for.

choices.text: Neither: `hits` has no dependencies, so 13 must be an error in the database
choices.why: The 13 are real entries against the standard library, which every Go program depends on; the fix is Go 1.27.2.

choices.text: The symbol scan, because `-scan module` only works on binaries
choices.why: `-scan module` ran on the source of `hits` in the transcript. It refuses a package pattern; it does not need a binary.

prompt: Every remaining finding on `hits` says `Fixed in: stdlib@go1.27.2`. What closes them?
hint: The standard library is not in `go.mod`'s requirements.

choices.text: `go get stdlib@go1.27.2`
choices.why: There is no module called `stdlib` to get. The name in the report is a label for the standard library, which comes with the toolchain.

choices.text: Installing Go 1.27.2 and rebuilding every binary
choices.why: Right. Under `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.2` the scan found nothing; the real fix is installing that release and replacing the binaries built with 1.27.1.

choices.text: `go mod tidy`, which refreshes every requirement to its newest patch
choices.why: `tidy` adds missing requirements and removes unused ones. It upgrades nothing, and it never touches the Go release.

choices.text: Nothing: standard-library entries are informational and never matter
choices.why: They matter as soon as code reaches one, and a server that calls `net/http` would. They are module-level for `hits` only because `hits` calls none of them.

prompt: After `go get golang.org/x/text@latest`, `govulncheck ./...` exits 0. The `accept-bin` on the server was built before the upgrade. What does a binary scan of it say?
hint: The binary carries its own record of the modules it was built with.

choices.text: Clean: the binary reads the module versions from the current `go.mod`
choices.why: A binary never reads `go.mod`; it carries the versions it was built with, and `go version -m` prints them.

choices.text: Still affected, `Found in: golang.org/x/text@v0.3.7`, until it is rebuilt
choices.why: Right. The scan exited 3 until `go build` replaced the file, and then 0. The upgrade reaches production only with the new binary.

choices.text: It cannot say anything without the source code
choices.why: Binary mode exists for exactly this case; it read the build record and the symbol table.

choices.text: Affected by 15 vulnerabilities, because old binaries lose their symbols
choices.why: The 15 came from the stripped build. An ordinary binary keeps its symbol table however old it is.

prompt: The CI job runs `govulncheck` on `push` and `pull_request`. Why does it also have a `schedule` trigger?
hint: Which of the two inputs to a scan can change on a day nobody commits?

choices.text: Scheduled runs are cheaper on GitHub's runners
choices.why: Cost is not the reason given; the scheduled run does the same work as any other.

choices.text: `govulncheck` caches results and needs a daily refresh
choices.why: Each run fetches what it needs from the database. There is no result cache to refresh.

choices.text: The database changes while the code does not
choices.why: Right. A commit that passed on Monday fails on Thursday when an entry for a function it always called is published, and the schedule finds it without waiting for an unrelated pull request.

choices.text: Pull requests from forks skip the vulnerability check
choices.why: Nothing in the job file says so; the reason for the schedule is about time, not about who opened the pull request.

prompt: `govulncheck ./...` exits 3 with a symbol-level finding in a module you require. Put the remediation in order.
hint: Find the path, find who chose the version, change it, prove nothing broke, prove it closed, ship.
items: read the full path with `-show traces`
run `go mod why -m` on the module to see what brings it in
`go get` the module at the fixed or the newest version
rebuild the binaries and replace the running ones

prompt: Which of these are limits of `govulncheck` that its documentation or this lesson's runs showed? Select all that apply.
hint: Three are limits; the other three are things it does not do at all.

choices.text: A call made through `reflect` is invisible to the source scan
choices.why: Right. Static analysis cannot see which function a reflective call will pick, so a path through it is missed.

choices.text: A stripped binary is reported at module-level precision
choices.why: Right. `accept-small` went from 1 finding to 15 because no function names were left to check.

choices.text: There is no way to mark a finding as accepted
choices.why: Right. The documentation lists the absence; a decision to live with a finding has to live outside the tool.

choices.text: It sends your source code to vuln.go.dev for analysis
choices.why: The analysis runs on your machine. By its documentation, the requests carry module paths and nothing about your code.

choices.text: It only checks the modules listed directly in `go.mod`
choices.why: It checks the whole build, standard library included: `hits` has no requirements and still got 13 entries at the module level.

choices.text: It ignores the standard library unless you pass `-std`
choices.why: There is no `-std` flag in `govulncheck -h`, and every scan in the lesson listed standard-library entries.

prompt: `go mod why -m golang.org/x/net` shows your code reaching it through `example.com/client`, whose newest release still requires a vulnerable `golang.org/x/net`. What fixes the finding today?
hint: Go builds with the highest version any module in the build asks for.

choices.text: Wait for `example.com/client` to publish a release that requires the fix
choices.why: That works eventually, and leaves the finding open until a stranger acts. Nothing stops you raising the version yourself.

choices.text: Fork `example.com/client` and point a `replace` directive at the fork
choices.why: Heavy, and unnecessary: the client's code does not change, only the version of a module it uses.

choices.text: `go get golang.org/x/net` at the fixed version in your own module
choices.why: Right. Minimal version selection takes the highest version anybody requires, so your requirement wins over the client's older one. Run the tests, because the client now runs on a version it was not released with.

choices.text: Delete `golang.org/x/net` from `go.sum`
choices.why: `go.sum` holds checksums, not choices; the next build puts the same line back.

prompt: A binary scan reports `Vulnerable symbols found: #1: language.ParseAcceptLanguage` where the source scan printed a trace. What can you not learn from the binary scan?
hint: What does a Go binary keep, and what does it throw away?

choices.text: Which version of the module is in the binary
choices.why: That it knows exactly: `Found in: golang.org/x/text@v0.3.7`, from the build record.

choices.text: Who calls it, and from where
choices.why: Right. A binary keeps function names but no call information, so there is no trace and no line of your code to go to.

choices.text: Whether the function is linked into the file at all
choices.why: That is exactly what the symbol table answers, and why the finding is at the symbol level.

choices.text: Which version fixes it
choices.why: The binary scan printed `Fixed in: golang.org/x/text@v0.3.8`, from the database, as the source scan did.
